title: A pricing page for a law practice
metaTitle: Law practice pricing page: show the fit
excerpt: A law practice pricing page should show the fee shape, what is included, and how to request a consultation. Clients use it to judge fit.
alt: A laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, beside a plant and a yellow mug, a working surface for a page that has to show a fee clearly.
caption: A desk set up to read the work, not to admire a texture. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Does a law firm have to publish hourly rates?
faqs.answer: Publish the shape of the fee even when a single rate would mislead. A fixed fee, an hourly estimate with the facts that move it, or a priced first phase all help a client judge fit. Print a number only when you will honor it, and check what your jurisdiction allows you to advertise.

faqs.question: What if every matter is different?
faqs.answer: Say so for the matters that truly have no public total, then price the part you can see. A first meeting, a letter review, or a defined draft is often enough for a client to judge fit. A page that only says to get in touch leaves the question they came with unanswered.

faqs.question: What should a pricing page ask the client to do?
faqs.answer: Ask them to request a consultation, and tell them what to send so you can confirm the shape. The kind of matter, the deadline, and the letter or draft in front of them are usually enough. The reply should say whether you can act, not offer legal advice by email.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A client choosing counsel under time pressure opens a law practice pricing page to judge fit. They want the shape of the fee, what sits inside it, and how to request a consultation. The arithmetic can wait until the matter is defined. Nielsen Norman Group's 2011 account of page visits is the reason to keep that answer short. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and on the pages they do open they have time to read only about a quarter of the text.

If every consultation starts with the same question about how you charge, the page should already have answered it. Hiding the shape behind "contact us" spends the only attention you are likely to get. Google's helpful-content guidance warns against pages that send people back to search to finish the job. A fee page that withholds the shape is one of those pages.

## Fit is the decision this page can actually make

The client is not there to multiply hours by a rate. They are deciding whether your way of charging matches the matter in their hands.

A shop owner with a renewal letter wants to know if a lease review is a defined piece of work. A founder in a co-owner dispute wants to know if the first step is advice on the letter, or an open-ended fight. A family sorting an estate wants to know if the first meeting is a paid hour or a short call to see if you can act. Those are fit questions. A total at the bottom of a calculator rarely is, because the matter is not known yet.

Write the page so a person can sort themselves in a minute. Name the matters you price in a repeatable way. Say which matters you will only scope after a conversation. Put the consultation request where that distinction is already clear.

A page that opens with a speech about the value of careful counsel delays the sort. Care can be visible in the scope itself. A defined review, a named limit, and a plain next step are the evidence.

## Show the shape, then the number if you have one

The shape is the thing a client remembers. Publish it even when the dollar figure varies.

Use shapes the client can picture.

- A fixed fee for a defined document or a defined meeting.
- Hourly work with a written estimate, and the two or three facts that move the estimate.
- A staged matter: a priced first phase, then a separate decision if the work continues.
- A retainer for a known volume, such as a set of contracts each quarter.
- A capped fee, with a sentence about what happens if the cap is reached before the work is finished.

Match each shape to a matter you actually take. A commercial lease review might be fixed for the first markup, then hourly if negotiation starts. An employment letter might be a fixed advice memo. A dispute that may go to a hearing might be staged, because nobody honest can price the whole path on day one.

Write the number when it is stable and you are willing to honor it. A fixed fee that is real is a gift to a client who is comparing firms between meetings. If the number moves with facts you do not have yet, publish the variables instead of a teaser. Number of parties. Urgency. Whether the other side already has a lawyer. Whether you are reviewing a draft or negotiating it. Page count, when page count truly changes the work.

Check the advertising rules of your jurisdiction before you publish a result, a guarantee, or a fee that could be read as a promise. The page can still describe the shape while you confirm what your regulator allows you to print.

## What is included, and what is not

A shape without a boundary is a slogan. For each matter you list, write two short lists.

Included might be: reading the papers they send, a conflict check, one meeting, and a letter or a marked-up draft. Say the actual deliverable. "Advice" is vague. "A marked-up lease and a one-page note of the three risks that matter" is a thing they can expect.

Left out might be: filing fees, a barrister, work in another jurisdiction, and a second phase you have not agreed. The excluded list is what makes the included list believable. Clients who have hired lawyers before are listening for the surprise. Name it.

Keep the lists in the client's words. "One round of changes on the draft you send" is clearer than "reasonable amendments." If a second round is common, say how it is charged. Silence on the second round is where trust leaks.

If disbursements are always extra, say that in the same view as the fee, not in a footnote set in gray. Court fees, search fees, and travel are not shameful. They are part of the fit. A client who cannot pay a filing fee needs to know before they request time.

## The consultation sits after the shape

The action on this page is to request a consultation, and the request should say what you need in order to confirm the shape.

Ask for the kind of matter, the deadline, and the document or the letter that prompted the search. Ask for the other party's name when you need it for a conflict check. Leave the life story for the conversation. A ten-field form between a clear fee and a human reply undoes the clarity you just earned.

Say what you will send back. Whether you can act. Which shape applies. What you need before work starts. A client under time pressure is also budgeting their week. "We reply on business days with a yes, a no, or a question" is a useful sentence if it is true. Do not print a speed you will not keep.

The confirmation should repeat the limit. The reply is not legal advice. It is a decision about fit. That protects the client from treating an email as counsel, and it protects the firm from being treated as already engaged.

## Write it so a quarter of the text is enough

Because readers get through only about a quarter of a typical page, the fee cannot depend on a paragraph they might skip.

Give each matter its own heading, in words they would say out loud. Put the shape in the first sentence under that heading. Put included and excluded in lists. Put the consultation link at the end of the block, and once at the top of the page for the person who already knows which matter they have.

Google's people-first questions are a direct test. After reading, can someone achieve the goal they arrived with? Here the goal is to judge fit and to ask for a consultation. If they still need a second search to learn how a lease review is charged, the page is unfinished, however elegant the type.

Avoid a single table of twelve matters that all say "bespoke." That grid hides the shapes inside a word that means "we will tell you later." Two or three matters, written fully, beat a matrix of identical cells. The services page can carry the longer list. This page carries the money.

## What to keep off this page

Several habits make a fee page look finished and still fail the client.

A teaser price that excludes the work they came for. If the low number is only the conflict check, do not let it read as the cost of the lease review.

Awards, marble, and a Latin line where the scope should be. The client did not come here to be impressed. They came to see if the engagement fits the week they are having.

A calculator that treats a dispute like a product with a quantity. Quantities work for a defined document. They mislead when the work depends on another person's lawyer.

A promise of outcome tied to a fee. "We win, you pay nothing" is a claim with legal and ethical weight. Leave it off unless it is precisely true, permitted where you practice, and explained with the exceptions in the same view.

A speech about being expensive for a reason, with no shape under it. Price confidence is the scope, written down.

## When you still cannot print a number

Some matters should not carry a public total. Multi-party litigation, regulatory investigations, and deals that change every week are poor candidates for a fixed public fee. Say that in plain language. Then price the piece you can see.

The first conference. The advice on the letter they have already received. The review of the draft in front of them. A client can buy that phase, learn what you are like to work with, and decide whether the next phase is one they want. That is fit. A blank page that says every matter is unique is a refusal to do the sorting they needed.

Once the shapes are honest, the next gap is usually the list of services itself. A fee means little if the work is still described as a capability. Read [what belongs on the services page](/blog/the-services-page-a-law-practice-actually-needs) so each offer has an outcome, a boundary, and a next step.

When you want help deciding which shapes are clear enough to publish, [book an intro call with Hanabi](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the matters you are asked about every week.
